sketches.mechanism: The `object` declaration creates a singleton — exactly one instance, ever, enforced by the language. Combined with Kotlin's `companion object`, which exists only inside another class and cannot outlive it.
sketches.resonance: A companion that can never be duplicated or replaced — the language guarantees there will only ever be one, bound forever to the class it inhabits.

sketches.mechanism: Rust's ownership system: calling `drop()` explicitly destroys a value, and any subsequent attempt to use it is a compile-time error — the borrow checker enforces that what is gone is truly gone.
sketches.resonance: The compiler itself refuses to let you reach for what has already been released, turning grief into a build error.

sketches.mechanism: TypeScript's `never` type represents values that can never occur; a function returning `never` is one that never completes. Assigning `never` to a variable means the variable can hold nothing.
sketches.resonance: A promise declared with the type that cannot be fulfilled — the type system itself proves that some things will never arrive.
